en: Furthermore, for this one who possesses the vows of Vajrasattva, there are two categories of downfalls: root downfalls and gross downfalls. They are as follows: For this one who possesses the vows of Vajrasattva, there are two types of downfalls: root downfalls and gross downfalls. How are they so?
The first root downfall is said to arise from insulting the true guru;

the second downfall is declared to be the transgression of the Sugata’s command. To cause distress to the mind of the sublime guru is taught as the first root downfall; to overstep the word of the Sugata is described as the second downfall.
The third [transgression] is the manifestation of faults out of anger toward one's vajra-brothers;
and the fourth is declared by the Victors to be the abandonment of loving-kindness toward sentient beings.
The third is to manifest one's faults out of anger toward one’s vajra siblings.
To abandon loving-kindness toward sentient beings—the Victor has declared this to be the fourth [offense].
The root of the Dharma is the thought of awakening; by abandoning it, the fifth [offense] occurs.
The sixth occurs through disparaging the Dharma, whether one's own or another's established tenet.
The root of the Dharma is the bodhicitta; abandoning it is the fifth [root downfall].
To disparage the doctrines of one's own or others' tenets is the sixth [fault].
And the seventh [offense] is from revealing secrets to beings who have not been ripened;
the eighth is from showing contempt for the aggregates, which consist of the nature of the five Buddhas, in those beings who have not been ripened.
Proclaiming secrets to sentient beings who are not yet fully matured is the seventh [transgression].
"The five aggregates are the self, the Buddha himself"—this is the eighth [fault] of disparaging him.
The ninth [fault] consists of doubt regarding phenomena that are pure by nature;
the tenth is considered to be the constant abandonment of corrupted loving-kindness resulting from that [doubt].
To harbor doubt regarding phenomena that are pure by nature is the ninth [fault].
To always maintain loving-kindness toward those who are malicious—this is the tenth.
In the Dharma which is devoid of beginning and end, the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) arises from conceptual construction;
the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) is said to exist among those beings who perform ancestral rites (śrāddha) due to the corruption of their minds.
Regarding phenomena that are without beginning or end, the conceptualization of them as such is the eleventh [type of ignorance].
The twelfth [offense] is to corrupt the minds of sentient beings who possess faith.
The thirteenth [transgression] occurs from not practicing the commitments as they are obtained;
the fourteenth occurs from loathing women, who are the very nature of wisdom.
The samaya substances are obtained exactly as they are; not relying [on them] is the thirteenth.
The fourteenth [chapter], concerning the disparagement of women, who are the very nature of wisdom.
Thus ends the root downfall.
This refers to the root downfall.
If a yogi forcibly enjoys a yoginī who is bound by the yoga-vow,
even through the mere act of violating her, the first gross transgression is said to have occurred.
Whichever yogin is preeminent in power among the yogins and those bound by the yogic vows, [he shall be the leader].
The first offense of the *sthūla* class is explained; therein, even making light of it constitutes one.
If one does not consecrate the nectars according to the rules prescribed in the Tantras,
a gross downfall of the second type arises for him.
Following what is taught in the tantras, even nectar that lacks blessings [is effective].
Its gross downfall is that which causes the second [downfall] to arise.
Due to quarreling during a *gaṇacakra* feast and thereby reviling the *samaya*, the third downfall is said to befall that yogin; it is called "gross" (*sthūla*).
To engage in dispute during the gaṇacakra, or to revile the samaya,
is explained as the third gross downfall of that yogin.
When one of impaired intellect, having seen the secret doctrine, does not conceal it, a gross transgression occurs for him by revealing it; that is the fourth.
Whenever one sees secret teachings, one should not conceal them with a mind of deceit or guile.
If one makes it clearly visible, it becomes the fourth offense of gross transgression.
To explain erroneously to those who are faithful, to sentient beings, or to those who delight in the secret Dharma, constitutes the fifth [offense], known as "gross."
Any sentient being who possesses faith and delights in the secret Dharma—
To speak erroneously constitutes the fifth offense of gross transgression.
If one dwells together with those who belong to the Śrāvaka vehicle for seven days,
a sixth grave offense, a very serious transgression, arises for him.
Those of the inferior Śrāvaka vehicle [should] dwell together for seven days.
From that, the downfall of gross misconduct arises; it is the sixth, which is extremely grave.
But if one, while yoga is not yet realized, possesses the conceit of being a lord of yogis,
for him there will undoubtedly be a gross downfall on the seventh stage.
Without certain knowledge of yoga, the mind of a yogin is filled with the pride of overestimation.
There is no doubt that its grave offense will become the seventh.
To disclose the secret Dharma to a being who is not a fit vessel and who delights in external phenomena constitutes the eighth grave offense for him.
Any sentient being who has become a suitable vessel, yet delights in external phenomena—
When one correctly explains the secret teachings, that constitutes a gross downfall.
It becomes the eighth itself.
Thus ends the section on gross transgressions.
This refers to the offense of grossness.

Therefore, a *samayin* who has been seized by two transgressions should, according to his ability, first provide gifts and food, and then, in the presence of a true guru, undertake the vows of Vajradhara as before—beginning with the confession of sins and the taking of the three refuges.

Therefore, having been seized by the two downfalls, one should first perform an offering preceded by giving a feast as much as possible in the absence of the samaya; then, in the presence of the sublime guru, one should confess sins and undertake the three refuges and so forth as before, and thus adopt the meditation on the Vajradhara.
This is the ritual for initiation along with its auxiliary practices, together with the traditional instructions. ||o||
Thus concludes the ritual for empowerment, together with its instructions and its retinue.
